article.title: Voices from Turkey: “The More Oppressive the Regime Gets, the More Resilient People Become”
article.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We are broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. As climate negotiations enter their crucial final days, dozens of human rights groups have urged Turkish authorities to release four LGBTQ activists ahead of a hearing that’s just begun at a court in Istanbul. They’re among dozens of human rights defenders who’ve been imprisoned or subjected to criminal investigations and a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ groups that began in September. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Turkish authorities also raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sözcü TV and took the channel off the air, while appointing a trustee to run the channel and its website. Four executives from that TV network have also been detained. Since last month, the two remaining opposition channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party, with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024. Despite the growing repression, here in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government marched alongside international civil society groups this weekend to mark the Global Day of Action. They are also gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups that’s taking place in another part of Antalya. We stopped by on Sunday, and I spoke to organizers of the People’s Climate Summit. This is Zişan Tokaç, an activist from Istanbul. ZIŞAN TOKAÇ: My name is Zişan. I am an organizer with the People’s Climate Summit. There are a lot of participants, from government agencies, from corporations, as well, under different badges, as well as from social movements around the world, and they are all in conference halls discussing the future of the climate. And we are here to say that there are people who are excluded from these conference halls. There are people who don’t have the right badges to enter those conference halls, and our voices are not heard in these conference halls. However, these people are also the exact people who are going to be impacted the most by climate change, or who are actively being impacted the most by climate change. So, what People’s Climate Summit does is to bring the people’s voices into the light of the media, the participants of COP31, and raise our demands, because our demands are very different from what governments and corporations want to agree on at these summits. AMY GOODMAN : That was Zişan Tokaç, an activist from Istanbul. We also spoke to Ecehan Balta from the Climate Justice Coalition. She’s based in Ankara and one of the many Turkish activists who’ve been denied entry into the COP this year. She’s a longtime academic and activist who’s worked with rural communities across Turkey fighting for their lands. I began by asking her if she could enter the U.N. climate summit, where we are. ECEHAN BALTA : Actually, I tried to get one. Actually, I got one for the green zone. Then they canceled without no reason. So — AMY GOODMAN : Who is they? ECEHAN BALTA : The Turkish government canceled my entrance to the green zone. So, we cannot be there. I mean, there are some friends and comrades inside trying to reach their voices to their leaders, to the leaders, but we are not one of them. I’m not one of them. AMY GOODMAN : Last year, we were in Belém, in Brazil. We were in the gateway to the Amazon. ECEHAN BALTA : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : Place us, for us, geographically and the kind of climate challenges you face here in Turkey. ECEHAN BALTA : This year in Turkey is in some different contexts. Especially it’s important that it’s — the summit is being held on the border of — on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, which is the almost hottest seas in the world, and it’s getting hot day by day because of the — and they are building a nuclear power plant very close to here, in Mersin, and that will also, you know, contribute the heat of the Mediterranean Sea. AMY GOODMAN : When people organize in Turkey around environmental issues, how does the government respond? ECEHAN BALTA : Actually, the response changes from the region to region. But in general, they attack people. And we generally try to use the processes of laws, and we try to get, you know, positive decisions from the courts. But they never apply, and they are decided by the companies. And they force people to get out from the mining areas, for example. It was the case in Akbelen. They are planning to take the people out from 43 villages, in order to expand the mining area. And we have the court cases. We have the positive decisions. But the government itself doesn’t apply them, and they force people with the — I mean, by the military force to get out from those regions. This is the general case in Turkey. AMY GOODMAN : Ecehan Balta from the Climate Justice Coalition, speaking to us at the People’s Climate Summit over the weekend, about 20 minutes from where we are at the U.N. climate summit. I also spoke to Ömer Madra, one of Turkey’s best-known voices on climate change. He’s a longtime climate activist and beloved broadcaster here in Turkey, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of what was for 29 years Turkey’s only independent community radio station, Açık Radyo, which means Open Radio. In November of 2024, Turkey’s High Commission of Television and Radio revoked Açık Radyo’s FM license after a guest on one of the shows used the phrase “Armenian genocide.” Turkish authorities initially imposed a five-day broadcast ban on the show, later pulled their FM license completely, based on claims that the station had failed to comply with the initial suspension. Forty days later, Açık Radyo, or Open Radio, was reborn as an online radio station called Apaçık Radyo, or Wide Open Radio. It had to open as a different name. I began by asking Ömer Madra why he started Open Radio, Açık Radyo, back in 1995. ÖMER MADRA : I mean, Açık Radyo, since its inception, has been actively engaged in the struggle against all these kinds of anti-democratic things. I mean, you know, my first street protest was in 1965, and now I’m on my 61st year of protesting in the streets. I’m a street boy, as you might — AMY GOODMAN : You’re now how old? Eighty-one? ÖMER MADRA : Eighty-one. More. Well, 81-and-a-half. I have always felt myself a member of the ’68 rebellion generation or revolutionary generation. AMY GOODMAN : And, in fact, Juan González was a part of that ’68 revolutionary change. I mean, he was one of the leaders of the Columbia student strike. He went on to co-found the New York chapter of the Young Lords, the Puerto Rican equivalent of the Black Panthers, and one of the great journalists of the United States. ÖMER MADRA : I’ve been following you with very much admiration, and very strictly, I should say. AMY GOODMAN : For a global audience, what should we understand about Turkey? ÖMER MADRA : Oh, it’s rather difficult. I mean, it has been under the real stress of authoritarianism, getting worse and worse all the time. This started as a democracy, you know, president at the time a former politician, Erdoğan. And he was a reformist in his — in his first three or four years, and maybe more than that. That’s why I believe he was reelected with his party. But then, in what we see in many other European countries, as well, and in very many parts of the world, in many countries, there has been a trend towards, if not fascism, but anti-democratic, and the government of Turkey also chose that path. And we have — I do believe that we have none other thing to do than to resist such thing and struggle for a full democracy all the time. AMY GOODMAN : So, you have a team coming to Antalya to cover the climate summit, COP31. You’re inside, and you’re outside the COP . How would you frame the climate issue, in Turkey and globally? ÖMER MADRA : The biggest problem is global climate change, of course, or global warming. But the second very big problem is that there is no free media to talk about this. Almost 90% of the Turkish people were not aware of COP or COP31. AMY GOODMAN : Apaçık Radyo, what it’s called now, very Wide Open Radio, is the same age as Democracy Now! It’s 30 years old. It’s more than — ÖMER MADRA : We’re a bit older. AMY GOODMAN : Oh, really? ÖMER MADRA : One — one year older. AMY GOODMAN : You think you’re more mature? ÖMER MADRA : Not mature, but our birthday is a bit — one year older. AMY GOODMAN : And I want to thank you for running Democracy Now! on your radio station, ÖMER MADRA : Amy, thank you so much. I mean, it’s my great pleasure. AMY GOODMAN : That’s Ömer Madra, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Apaçık Radyo, or Wide Open Radio. It used to be called Open Radio, or Açık Radyo, until it was taken off the airwaves two years ago, is now available online. For more on the state of repression and dissent here in Turkey, we’re joined now by Berkan Özyer, the director of Greenpeace Türkiye. Thanks so much for being with us. Usually, you deal with environmental issues, but I want you to talk about this level of pressure. I mean, even in the midst of the U.N. climate summit, two Turkish opposition stations are taken over by the Turkish government. And in the lead-up to it, if you can explain what’s happened to many dissenters, and especially the LGBTQ community? BERKAN ÖZYER: Welcome. Thank you. First, it depends on how you look at the things. From the eyes of a person who actually lives here, and this — this trend goes on for years. And also, if you look at the bigger picture, it’s also another global trend starting to get accelerated also. So, as Turkey, we are one of the, let’s say, pioneers of this unfortunate global trend. So, but the main thing is, because of the lack of leader in the leadership, there’s a power vacuum within this system in terms of values, so there is no one to judge. Even when you are hosting hundreds-plus world leaders in your own city, in your own country, you can also still do this, because there is no one to, you know, judge you or make you pay a price. But on the contrary, there is another point we need to focus. Just like to People’s Summit — you were there — this also, the more oppressive regime gets, the more resilient people become. This is the most important part for us, as well, because as we saw in the streets of Antalya, as we have been seeing in the streets of many different cities of Turkey, there is a popular demand for a change. Whether it should be about environment, whether it should be about women issues or LGBTQ movements, there is a demand for change. And it will be happening. And we want to make it real when it happens. AMY GOODMAN : And, I mean, there was a mass protest on Saturday, thousands of people, but it was international. And it seemed like the Turkish dissidents within the protesters felt safer, even with the rainbow flag, waving it, because they felt protected by this international mass protest. BERKAN ÖZYER: Exactly. This is like the old saying: “Together, we stand.” You know, it goes for the same country, as well, but on the global stage also. The system, especially focused on securitization, wants to feel us alone, you know, insecure. But when you come together with your comrades, your friends from all around the world, from all around the city, as we saw just couple of days ago here in the streets of Antalya, you see that we are not alone in these fights, in the struggle against changing the system. This was a great example for us, as well. AMY GOODMAN : And last question on the environment. You are the head of Greenpeace Türkiye. Explain coal phaseout, why also Turkey has become the largest importer of plastic waste from the EU, from the European Union. BERKAN ÖZYER: Two things: lack of monitors, lack of audits, and lack of system. This is the biggest thing. Coal is very, how to say, bad for the environment, air pollution, human health issues, soil, water. It is bad for environment, and especially for economic reasons, as well. If you have a socioeconomic crisis like we do in Turkey, the price becomes even more higher. So, there has to be a coal phaseout announced immediately. This is the first thing we are asking. And second, we’ve become the biggest plastic waste importer from the EU and the U.K., as Turkey, because it was China up until 2018, and they put a ban on it, and then Turkey replaced due to logistic reasons. And it’s a dirty business. There is a lot of informalities around this. There is a lot of human rights abuse about this. So, this has to be — and also, you know, it gives you, gives your image — it expresses your stance in your position about the global trade. So, we don’t want to be none of — we don’t want any other country to export plastic waste of other countries. This is against — a fight against the whole plastic industry itself. The root cause is the plastic industry, and we are against it. AMY GOODMAN : Berkan Özyer, I want to thank you so much for being with us, director of Greenpeace here in Turkey. Coming up, Colombia’s former environment minister. She chaired the landmark Santa Marta Conference earlier this year on transitioning away from fossil fuels. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Music performed at last week’s World Leaders’ Summit for COP31. Page 2 This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit — that’s COP31, conference of parties, 31 years — here in Antalya, Turkey. Over 90,000 people have participated in this summit over the last week and a half. It’s considered the largest. Negotiators have just a few more days to see if they can come to some final agreement. Despite all the many significant issues being debated here, from climate finance to electrification, what’s not discussed is also significant, and that’s the transition away from fossil fuels, the number one driver of global warming. Well, seven months ago, a bloc of nations led by Colombia held a separate conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, with the explicit shared agenda to begin the transition away from fossil fuels. More than 50 countries participated. A group of countries have already released national roadmaps to do just that. Colombia is a significant fossil fuel producer. The country is Latin America’s largest coal exporter, as well as a significant exporter of crude oil. Despite the importance of the fossil fuel industry for Colombia’s economy, the Santa Marta Conference was championed by then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro, whose term ended in August. Colombia’s new right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella has since withdrawn Colombia from the Santa Marta coalition. But the larger process continues. We’re joined now by Irene Vélez-Torres. As Colombia’s acting minister of environment and sustainable development under Petro, she served as co-chair for the Santa Monica Conference along with the Netherlands. She was also the former director of Colombia’s National Environmental Agency and the former minister of mines and energy. We thank you so much for being with us. Those are a lot of titles that you don’t have right now because of the new government in Colombia. But you’re here to represent the Santa Marta coalition. First, the significance of your new president pulling out of the Santa Marta coalition? And explain what it is. IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : The Santa Marta coalition unites 57 governments, but also civil society, subnational governments, parliamentarians, NGOs, who came together in Santa Marta with a very specific, clear message, which is it is needed and urgent to phase out fossil fuels. And because here in these COPS we have the limitation of consensus, then we needed a different — AMY GOODMAN : Which it really isn’t. Consensus is not actually the rule. It’s just the custom. But to make clear to people around the world, fossil fuels are not mentioned when it comes to final documents at the COP summit, which might shock people. IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is really strange for someone that is not part of this diplomatic world to actually know that 80% of the global emissions are connected to fossil fuels, and however, climate change being discussed in these COPs is not addressed from the production and consumption of fossil fuels. The production side of this problem has always been denied. And why is that? Because there are lobbyists, there are petro lobbyists, people here defending the interest of the corporations, and therefore the discussions cannot make any progress. The agreements cannot even mention the word “fossil fuels.” AMY GOODMAN : So, talk about what’s come out of the Santa Marta coalition. You are releasing a report this week. We just heard, after yesterday’s broadcast of Democracy Now! , that countries like Spain are releasing a roadmap. What does that mean? A roadmap to what? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : One year ago, when we were in Belém in the COP30, we were very frustrated, because we couldn’t address the elimination of fossil fuels as part of the dialogues and as part of the official agenda. So, we decided, led by President Petro, that it was needed to create a parallel but connected space. And we decided to host that particular space, to create that particular space in Santa Marta, Colombia. We managed to gather 57 countries with one agreement in order to get there, that the elimination of fossil fuels was necessary and that we needed to do it in an orderly and urgent way. We invited not only governments, but also civil society and subnational governments. And when we were there, we decided that the transition away from fossil fuels had three calls of action: one, to make roadmaps, which implies to plan; second, that the decarbonization of trade is needed, particularly for oil, coal and gas-producing countries like Colombia; and third, that the financial system has to be revised, because, otherwise, especially countries from the Global South won’t have the investment needed in order to make the diversification of economies that are necessary as part of the just transition. So, we have these three work streams already in progress, and we hope that towards the second conference, that is going to take place in Tuvalu in July 2027, we can show more action-oriented decisions by the governments. AMY GOODMAN : When you say “climate finance,” another buzzword that most people don’t understand — loss and damage is within that — if you can explain what it is, what it means when you have the historically biggest carbon polluters in the world, from the United States to China, and those countries feeling the terrible effects then, though not causing it? What is a fair way to help these countries adapt, but also deal with catastrophes, like Nepal — IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : — with a glacier breaking off and killing thousands of people? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes, 31 COPs have been trying to address the problem of financiating actions that could cope with climate change. What kind of actions? Most of them are focused on adaptation, which means to have the tools at the national level to cope with the changes that the increase in global temperatures are going to generate. It was maybe three COPs ago that we also came with the concept of the Loss and Damage Fund, which will mean that all developed countries, the ones that have polluted the most, will put money in a bag, and every country that will feel damages generated by climate change will be able to address that fund. However, the fund is insufficient, and the mechanisms to address that money are super complicated, bureaucratic, very difficult for countries to actually get to those resources. But there is another, blind coronary that I want to point here, which is that this finance is not meant for the diversification of economies, which means that there is no allocation of money for transitioning from producing gas, oil and coal to producing something different, which means that our economic dependency is not really overcome with the kind of finance that is offered in these COPs. AMY GOODMAN : The Colombian government and the U.S. government have signed two new agreements around critical minerals and nuclear energy. What is the significance of this? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is a terrible news for Colombia and its sovereignty. Basically, what happened there is that the Colombian government resigned to sovereignty. And there are particularities about that agreement that should be clearly stated. One, the Colombian government has made explicit that it’s going to ask permission to the U.S. in order to allocate any mining project, which means that it’s like if we were the son that has to ask for permission in order to act, and not a proper government, not a proper state. The second, all the knowledge generated by Colombia as a sovereign country will have to be shared with the U.S., meaning that we don’t have knowledge sovereignty and that everything that is our resources in the subsoil will be known by the U.S. And the third one is that any investment that the U.S. would like to prioritize will have to be also prioritized by Colombia. AMY GOODMAN : Final comments? We have 20 seconds. What people should know around the world about what you want to see come out of COP31? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Let me also say that this government of Colombia has just reversed the protection of the Amazon. Gustavo Petro already had protected 42% of our territory, declaring it a fossil-free zone. And however, this government came and reversed that historical decision, not only for Colombia, but for all the South American countries that share this biome. This is making a huge risk in terms of water integrity, because the water that is generated by the forest of the Amazon also moves towards Bogotá. So, what we are seeing is really an ecocide taking place in Colombia. AMY GOODMAN : Irene Vélez-Torres, former director of Colombia’s National Environmental Agency, also served as Colombia’s acting minister of the environment under President Gustavo Petro. She co-chaired the Santa Marta Conference earlier this year. Coming up, Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at Union of Concerned Scientists. And then we’ll talk about what’s happening in Ecuador. We’re at the U.N. climate summit. Back in a minute. [break] AMY GOODMAN : For our radio listeners, that music break was recorded at the — for our radio listeners, that musical break was recorded at the “Polluters Must Pay” protest here at COP31 in Antalya this morning. In the video, protesters dressed as giant peanuts. Yes, peanuts. They’re dancing while holding up giant pennies that spell out “Pay Up.” A recurring chant at the protest was “Billions, not peanuts,” “Trillions, not peanuts.” They were protesting the inadequate funding and contributions from rich, polluting countries to the countries that need adaptation and recovery funds the most. Page 3 As Democracy Now! continues broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, we speak with Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, about climate finance — the notion that efforts to mitigate the climate crisis must be funded. “Climate finance is not an abstract thing. It’s what countries need to be able to transition away from fossil fuels,” says Cleetus. “And right now we have pennies in these funds.” She notes that at a pledging event for the Adaptation Fund, which supports climate finance for developing countries, a mere $50 million was pledged. “It’s shameful, absolutely unjust, what’s happening here. And richer countries are continuing to block progress.” This comes as scientists say the world is set to overshoot the target, set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, of limiting global heating to 1.5 degrees Celsius. Page 4 Ecuadorians voted overwhelmingly in 2023 to stop oil extraction at Yasuní National Park, one of the most biodiverse places on Earth, yet oil drilling has continued despite that historic referendum. “The government does not want to close the wells,” says Ivonne Yánez, the president of Acción Ecológica, an environmental nonprofit group based in Ecuador. The Ecuadorian government is also “continuing expanding the oil activities in the Amazon,” she points out. Yánez also speaks about how dangerous Latin America is for environmental activists. It is where “the most number of defenders that are just defending their lands, their rivers, their rights,” are killed. “And in Ecuador, this is also happening.”
